records.name: Wyoming
records.current_summary: Wyoming signed public-facility bans in March 2025. A July 2026 per-state legal-risk assessment lists it among 'the worst states' for legislation targeting transgender adults.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (404 - MAP has retired/moved this equality-map entry); the underlying Movement Advancement Project equality-map page carried the authoritative per-state list of bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities matching their gender identity, with the year each was enacted (the dossier's per-state facility-ban years come from it). For Wyoming it documents the facility bans signed in March 2025.

Erin In The Morning's July 2026 anti-trans legal-risk assessment map for transgender travellers (Erin Reed; republished 27 Aug 2026 by a regional LGBTQ outlet), built from 5 years of daily legislative tracking with a rubric for the worst bills. Wyoming is listed among 'the worst states' for legislation targeting transgender adults. Also documents that federal policies keep creating legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.

sources.title: Governor signs bathroom bills mandating who can use which facilities | News Letter Journal (Wyoming News Exchange)
sources.claim: Wyoming News Exchange report that on Monday, March 3, 2025, Gov. Mark Gordon signed two facility measures into law: House Bill 72, the 'Protecting privacy in public spaces act,' covering sex-designated restrooms, showers, sleeping quarters and locker rooms at public facilities, and Senate File 62, 'Sex-designated facilities and public schools,' requiring public school children, pre-kindergarten and up plus charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth. SF 62 requires districts to provide a 'reasonable accommodation' to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth. For this record: confirms both of Wyoming's March 2025 facility bans, naming the two statutes, the signing date and each law's scope.

records.name: West Virginia
records.current_summary: March 2025 facility ban with unusually wide reach: K-12, higher education, corrections and domestic-violence shelters. In the worst-law group per the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Below the national score 0.36.

sources.claim: MAP (Movement Advancement Project) equality-map page cataloguing state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity; the dossier cites it for the facility-ban enumeration. NOTE: the URL returned a 404 page at fetch time (MAP has since moved the page).

Erin In The Morning, 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map: July 2026' (Stonewall News, published 27 Aug 2026): a per-state legal-risk grading of anti-trans law. The adult map lists 'Do Not Travel (FL, ID, KS, TX)' and 'The Worst States (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY)' - this state is in the worst group. The update records Idaho's promotion to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban (up to 5 years; partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists), Kansas's bounty-hunter civil-suit regime, and a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'.

sources.title: Morrisey signs bill defining 'man' and 'woman' into law | WV MetroNews
sources.claim: Local Capitol report that on Wednesday, March 12, 2025, Gov. Patrick Morrisey signed Senate Bill 456, the 'Riley Gaines Act,' which defines a 'woman' as an adult human of the female sex and a 'man' as an adult human of the male sex and aims to preserve women's single-sex spaces, primarily locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centers, dormitories and prisons. The state Senate passed the bill on March 3 and the House of Delegates passed it on March 6, with Morrisey saying at the signing that bathrooms, locker rooms, domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centers 'should be kept private for women only.' For this record: confirms the March 2025 West Virginia facility-restriction statute, its unusually wide facility reach (including corrections and domestic-violence shelters) and the exact signing date.

records.name: Arkansas
records.current_summary:
Arkansas confines trans students to birth-sex school facilities under a March 2023 law (HB 1156) that remains in force and was extended in 2025; its school focus means visitor exposure is narrower than in states with adult-reaching bans.

Its ban on gender-affirming care for minors remains in litigation (en-banc review of an injunction reversal pending), and the July 2026 per-state legal-risk grading lists Arkansas among the worst states.

The adult map lists 'Do Not Travel (FL, ID, KS, TX)' and 'The Worst States (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY)' - this state is in the worst group. The update records Idaho's promotion to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban (up to 5 years; partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists), Kansas's bounty-hunter civil-suit regime, and a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'.

sources.title: LGBTQIA+ rights in Arkansas - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's LGBTQIA+ rights in Arkansas page records that a bathroom bill became law on 11 April 2023 (Act 619), making Arkansas the fourth state to restrict trans students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender, and that it was amended/extended in 2025. The page also notes Arkansas was the first state (2021) to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans minors, a law a federal judge enjoined for 'irreparable harm' to minors while litigation continued, and that state law has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981. Confirms the record's account of the 2023 school-facility law and the still-litigated care ban.

sources.title: Arkansas becomes the first state to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans youth - LGBTQ Nation
sources.claim: LGBTQ Nation (March 2021) reported that Arkansas became the first state to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans youth after the legislature overrode the governor's veto of the ban, which critics at the time called 'the single most extreme anti-trans law to ever pass through a state legislature.' This is the same 2021 care ban whose court challenge the record describes as still in litigation.

freshness_all.fact: March 2023 school bathroom law (signed by Gov. Sanders) still in force; care-ban litigation ongoing (en banc review of injunction reversal) - facility claim current.

records.name: Ohio
records.current_summary:
Ohio enacted a law in 2024 governing public bathroom and facility use by sex assigned at birth, recorded in a national equality tracker of such bans (the tracker's page has since moved from its cited URL).

An independent July 2026 legal-risk assessment of anti-trans legislation lists Ohio among its 'worst states' group for transgender adults, alongside most of the Deep South and several Plains and Mountain states; the same assessment's frame is 'Worst Policies In Effect' nationally.

The adult map lists 'Do Not Travel (FL, ID, KS, TX)' and 'The Worst States (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY)' - this state is in the worst group. The update records Idaho's promotion to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban (up to 5 years; partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists), Kansas's bounty-hunter civil-suit regime, and a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'.

sources.title: Gov. DeWine signs bill limiting bathroom use by trans people at Ohio schools, colleges | The Statehouse News Bureau
sources.claim: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed the measure on Nov. 27, 2024; under the new law all K-12 schools and colleges must require students to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching the gender on their birth certificates. The article identifies Senate Bill 104 as the legislative vehicle and notes the bill also designates public and private school bathrooms and other facilities such as locker rooms by sex. For this record: dated confirmation of Ohio's 2024 facility-use law as enacted and signed.

sources.title: Ohio Gov. DeWine signs bill restricting transgender students' use of bathrooms | PBS News
sources.claim: AP report that on Nov. 27, 2024 Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed the 'Protect All Students Act,' signing out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil rights groups. The measure requires public and private schools, colleges and universities to designate separate bathrooms, locker rooms and overnight accommodations 'for the exclusive use' of either males or females based on sex assigned at or near birth; it takes effect in 90 days and contains no enforcement mechanism, with sponsor Republican state Sen. Jerry Cirino. Documents the scope (K-12 through college) and 90-day clock of the state's new facility restriction.

sources.title: Ohio Governor Signs 'Bathroom Bill' Into Law, Impacting K-12 Schools and Higher Education Institutions in the State - Ogletree
sources.claim: Law-firm client alert: on Nov. 27, 2024, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed Senate Bill 104, officially the 'Protect All Students Act' but widely coined the 'Bathroom Bill,' which outlines specific guidelines and restrictions for the use of restrooms, locker rooms, changing rooms and shower rooms in Ohio schools, with an effective date of Feb. 25, 2025. Independent legal reading of the statute's facility restriction and its implementation timeline for schools and colleges.

records.name: Iowa
records.current_summary:
Iowa enacted a public-facility-use law in 2023 and bans state-funded gender-affirming care for minors; a September 2026 status check confirmed both remain in force, while the Iowa Supreme Court struck down the parallel ban on surgery coverage for adults — a partial carve-back.

An independent July 2026 legal-risk assessment lists Iowa among its 'worst states' group for transgender adults.

Independent analysts of the same period caution that legal-risk grades predict how the state behaves toward trans people, not how residents do, and that recorded violence counts are undercount floors.

sources.claim: MAP (Movement Advancement Project) equality-map page cataloguing state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity; the dossier cites it for Iowa's enacted facility ban and the 18-state group defining sex as biological sex (Iowa not among the states listed there as defining sex by birth in statute). NOTE: URL returned a 404 at fetch time (MAP has moved the page).

Erin In The Morning, 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map: July 2026' (Stonewall News, published 27 Aug 2026): a per-state legal-risk grading of anti-trans law. The adult map lists 'Do Not Travel (FL, ID, KS, TX)' and 'The Worst States (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY)' - this state is in the worst group. The update records Idaho's promotion to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban (up to 5 years; partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists), Kansas's bounty-hunter civil-suit regime, and a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'.

'Safe states don't make safer people' (The Needle, July 2026): data essay overlaying the state legal-risk map on Trans Murder Monitoring killings data - legal-risk grades predict how the state behaves, not how people behave toward trans people; every count is an undercount; rates do not line up with the map. Cited as interpretive context for reading a state's mid-map legal-risk position (Iowa not named in the fetched text).

sources.title: Iowa enacts transgender bathroom bill and ban on gender-affirming care for minors
sources.claim: Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds signed two bills on March 22, 2023: Senate File 538 bars doctors from administering gender-affirming care to anyone under 18 (covering puberty blockers, hormone therapy and transition-related surgeries), and Senate File 482 prevents transgender students from entering school bathrooms or changing rooms that correspond with their gender identities. The restroom restriction applies to multiperson restrooms and locker rooms at public and private elementary and secondary schools and took effect immediately, with single-person facilities available to trans students who obtain written consent from legal guardians. Names both statutes behind this record's Iowa summary.

sources.title: Iowa Supreme Court Says Medicaid Must Cover Care for Transgender People | American Civil Liberties Union
sources.claim: On March 8, 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Good v. Iowa Dept. of Human Services that the state discriminated against two transgender women by denying their Medicaid claims for transition-related surgery, holding that excluding Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming surgery violates the Iowa Civil Rights Act. Documents the Iowa court carve-back of the state's surgery-coverage ban for adults that this record references.

sources.title: A Timeline of Litigation for Coverage of Gender-Affirming Transgender Surgery in Iowa - ACLU of Iowa
sources.claim: ACLU of Iowa's litigation timeline for coverage of gender-affirming transgender surgery in the state, from the lawsuit filed on behalf of Mika Covington and Aiden Vasquez over Iowa Medicaid's refusal to cover medically necessary gender-affirming surgery, through the March 2019 Iowa Supreme Court ruling and the litigation that followed. Tracks the state-court path that kept Medicaid surgery coverage available to transgender adults in Iowa.

sources.title: Iowa schools are scrambling to comply with new transgender bathroom law - KTVZ
sources.claim: KCCI (Des Moines) reporting syndicated by KTVZ: Gov. Kim Reynolds signed SF 482 into law on March 22, 2023, requiring anyone in an Iowa school, including students, staff, parents and visitors, to use only restrooms and other changing areas that correspond with the biological sex listed on their birth certificate, and Iowa school districts are scrambling to comply as the restriction takes effect. States the exact statute and subject scope (everyone on school grounds) behind Iowa's public-facility-use law.

freshness_all.fact: 2023 bathroom bill + minor care ban remain in force; nuance: Iowa Supreme Court struck down the ban on surgery coverage for adults.

records.name: South Carolina
records.current_summary: 2024 facility ban expanded in 2026 to colleges and universities, raising its tier to “Worst Laws Passed” in the July 2026 assessment; part of the 18-state birth-sex-definition group. Below the national score 0.36.

sources.claim: July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: South Carolina is called out for expanding its bathroom ban to universities (campus settings added to the pre-existing restriction); the assessment's rubric ranks states on adult and youth law severity by reading bills, and South Carolina's expansion places it among the escalating states rather than the harshest tier.

ACLU of South Carolina (May 18, 2026): Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on Friday May 15, 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth; ACLU frames it as discrimination against trans students in K-12 and higher education and notes the Senate amended the bill before passage. Press release dated May 18, 2026.

records.name: Nebraska
records.current_summary: Gubernatorial executive order narrowing “male”/“female” and ending state recognition of trans people — mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state machinery against gender identity. Below the national score 0.36.
records.current_localsOnly: The executive order's direct bite is on state legal recognition - birth records, marker documentation and how state systems read a trans person's legal sex - which is resident-facing; what a visitor feels is the signal that state machinery is aimed at gender identity.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (publisher returns 403 to automated fetches); the underlying Hill report covers the governor signing an executive order narrowing the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female' and ending state recognition of transgender people.

sources.title: Governor Pillen Establishes Women's Bill of Rights by Executive Order | Office of Governor Jim Pillen
sources.claim: Governor's office announcement: on Aug. 30, 2023 Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed an executive order establishing the Women's Bill of Rights, making him the second U.S. governor to sign such an order 'declaring the biological definition of male and female.' The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms and states that a person's biological sex is defined at birth. Primary state-government source for Nebraska's sex-definition policy.

sources.title: Nebraska governor signs contentious executive order defining 'male' and 'female' - JURIST - News
sources.claim: Legal-news report: Nebraska Executive Order No. 23-16 signed Aug. 30, 2023 defines the terms sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating there are biological differences between males and females in athletic abilities and safety that warrant sex-based segregation for some athletic, social and educational spaces. Reports that opponents questioned the order's scope and legality, and links the order text itself.

sources.title: Nebraska governor signs executive order specifically defining females, males
sources.claim: Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed an executive order on Aug. 30, 2023 establishing a Women's Bill of Rights, declaring a 'biological definition of male and female' and detailing the distinctions state agencies must apply. Local Nebraska news confirmation of the signing date and content of the executive order this record is about.

records.name: Kentucky
records.current_summary:
Kentucky enacted a school-focused facility restriction in 2023 (K-12), recorded in two national trackers of transgender facility-access laws. Both tracker pages have since become unreachable at their cited URLs, so the entry rests on the research dossier's verbatim extract — the weakest evidentiary basis on this map.

For a visitor, direct exposure is limited by the law's school setting, but the statute places Kentucky in the group of states that have legislated against transgender facility use.

sources.claim: Movement Advancement Project equality-map page cataloguing, state by state, bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity; it lists this state's 2023 K-12 facility ban (the map data renders client-side, so the per-state entries were read via the dossier rather than the cached HTML).

sources.title: Kentucky Legislature overrides Beshear veto and passes anti-transgender law
sources.claim: Louisville Public Media: on March 29, 2023 the Kentucky legislature overrode Gov. Andy Beshear's veto, enacting Senate Bill 150, which bans gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors in Kentucky and restricts which bathrooms those students can use in public schools. Names the single 2023 statute that carries the K-12 school facility restriction this record is about, with the override date and bill number.

sources.title: Kentucky Department of Education releases guidance for districts on implementing anti-LGBTQ rules | WKMS
sources.claim: The Kentucky Department of Education in April 2023 released guidance for school districts implementing the new anti-LGBTQ rules, advising districts to remove sex education from fifth-grade curriculum and to tread cautiously with the bathroom-ban provisions. Confirms the school-side operation of Kentucky's 2023 facility restriction and that K-12 districts were the implementing bodies.

sources.title: Kentucky's ban on gender-affirming care takes effect as federal judge lifts injunction | PBS News
sources.claim: On July 14, 2023, U.S. District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, allowing Kentucky's ban on gender-affirming care for minors to take effect and preventing transgender minors from accessing puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law, and the ACLU of Kentucky called the ruling a temporary setback. Dated outcome of federal litigation over the same 2023 statute that contains the school bathroom restriction.
